title: The license test, the local stack and Lab 1
part: Part 3 · AI as your co-admin, behind gates
brief: Read the LICENSE before anything runs on your machine. Then the same broken nginx three ways: in the browser, by hand in Docker, and with the agent.

exercises.prompt: Sort these tools. Which are OSI-approved open source, going by their LICENSE files on 31 Oct 2026?
exercises.explain: Claude Code's LICENSE.md says 'All rights reserved'. Crush is FSL-1.1-MIT, source-available but not OSI. Warp's client went AGPL in April 2026 but the AI tier phones home. Ansible Lightspeed is a Red Hat subscription. Teach the proprietary ones as what you will meet at work, not as the stack.
exercises.cite: Author's research notes, research/open-source-ai-tools-linux-admin.md (not published in this repo yet)

exercises.prompt: Which two open-weight models does the course ship as defaults, and why those two?
options: Qwen3-coder and GLM, because they score highest
devstral:24b and gpt-oss:20b, because their Apache-2.0 weight licenses were verified at the source
Llama 3.3 70B and Gemma 3, because they are the most popular
Any model Ollama lists; licenses do not matter locally
exercises.explain: Qwen and GLM may be fine, but their weight licenses could not be verified from a primary source, so they are not defaults. Local does not mean license-free.

exercises.prompt: A local open-weight model is safer against prompt injection than a cloud model, because your data never leaves the machine. True or false?
exercises.explain: False. Local inference buys sovereignty, not resistance to manipulation: in LogJack, Llama 3.3 70B obeyed poisoned logs 86% of the time, and open-weight models also hallucinate package names more often. The control is the gate, not the model.

exercises.prompt: Lab 1, by hand first. Fix this nginx.conf so nginx would parse it, / serves /var/www/app, /health returns 200 with the body ok, and /private/ is not served. Fix it; do not replace it.
exercises.hint: Four faults: worker_processes takes auto or a number; the root line is missing its semicolon; /health returns the wrong status and body; /private/ aliases a directory it should deny (and lists it). Read tests/test.sh in the lab for what the container checks.
exercises.explain: All static checks pass. The real judge is the container: make lab01 runs nginx -t and curl against your fix, and the hidden tests check the final state, never the commands you typed.

checks.name: worker_processes is a value nginx accepts (auto or a number)
the root directive ends with a semicolon
edited, not replaced (events, http, mime.types, server kept)

exercises.prompt: Before the agent runs on Lab 1 you run `run.sh validate`. What two things must it prove?
options: The model is loaded and the GPU is free
A no-op fails the tests and the oracle solution passes them
The container builds and nginx starts
The agent config is valid JSON
exercises.explain: That is the Harbor rule from Terminal-Bench. A task where doing nothing passes, or where the reference fix fails, measures nothing. This learnbook applies the same rule to itself: ./lb validate proves every broken file fails and every solution passes.

exercises.prompt: Run Lab 1 by hand, for real. Cleared when results.csv shows a manual run passing 9/9.
exercises.hint: Needs Docker. Type exit inside the container when /tests/test.sh passes; the timing is recorded either way.

exercises.prompt: Now the agent, on the local model. Approve each command. Cleared when an agent run passes 9/9; then compare the two timings honestly.
exercises.hint: Expect the local model to be slower than you and to try nginx -s reload before nginx -t. That is the lesson, not a failure of the lab.
